_note: Narrative for the General OT Security Posture report. Boilerplate and domain text inserted VERBATIM; data lines composed ONLY from templates. The generator must not free-write prose.

boilerplate.report_intro: This report gives management a high-level view of the operational technology security posture of {clientName}, as an early indication of strengths, weaknesses and priorities. It is based on a structured interview covering seven domains, and the question-by-question detail is in the companion workbook.
boilerplate.about_instrument: Each question is scored on the consultant's judgement of the answer given, so the grade reflects what could be established in conversation and has not been technically verified. It is an indicative read, and is neither a conformance assessment against a standard such as ISA/IEC 62443 nor a regulatory assessment.
boilerplate.how_to_read: Each question is scored on a four-point scale, from not in place to fully in place and managed, using the consultant's judgement of the answer. Questions are grouped into seven domains, and each domain receives a grade. The overall grade starts from the average across the domains and is then held down so that it can never sit more than two grades above the weakest domain, and the top grade is given only when every domain reaches it. An area in poor shape therefore drags the headline down sharply rather than being averaged away. A coverage figure shows how many questions could be answered. Where coverage is low, the grade is shown as indicative only and should be confirmed. Questions answered as unknown reduce coverage rather than counting as a failure, and questions that do not apply are excluded.
boilerplate.method: The assessment was carried out as a structured interview with site, engineering and security staff, supported by any documents and observations available at the time. Each scored answer reflects the consultant's judgement of the response given. [Consultant to confirm or adjust this description so it matches how the session was run.]
boilerplate.limitations: This is a point-in-time, interview-based assessment of what could be established in the time available and from the evidence offered. It does not verify controls in technical depth, which is the role of the detailed assessments. Where coverage was low or answers were uncertain, the grade should be treated as provisional.
boilerplate.indicative_grade_caveat: The grade in this report is an indicative, high-level read based on a structured interview and the evidence available at the time. It does not measure conformance against ISA/IEC 62443 or any other standard, and it is not a regulatory assessment. Its purpose is to show where the organisation's operational technology security stands and where to look first; conformance is established by the detailed assessments that follow in the priority areas.
boilerplate.unknown_explained: An Unknown answer has not been used to push a domain's capability score up or down. Not knowing is treated as a finding about visibility and not as a known gap in control, so the lowest capability band (0, Not in place) remains the worst capability score and Unknown does not sit below it. Unknown answers do reduce the coverage figure, and they lower confidence in the resulting grade. A 'Low' or 'Moderate' confidence note next to a grade means that a meaningful share of the questions in that domain, or overall, could not be answered with certainty.
boilerplate.series_context: Its purpose is to point at the areas where a detailed assessment against ISA/IEC 62443, the NCSC CAF or whichever regime applies will be worth the effort.

executiveSummary._note: Composed by slot-substitution only; boilerplate inserted VERBATIM; consultant blocks seeded with data-derived facts plus a marked placeholder. No free-writing. Posture aim: an indicative capped-average headline grade to show quickly where to look first - NOT a conformance or regulatory determination. Order: verdict, scope, gap_shape, weakest-domain method + indicative, path_forward + confidence.

gapConcentrationFragments.lowCoverage: Coverage was below the threshold in {lowCoverageList}, so those domains are reported as indicative only.

boilerplate.exec_weakest_domain: The headline grade starts from the average across the graded domains and is then held down by two rules. It can never sit more than two grades above the weakest domain, and the top grade is awarded only where every domain reaches it. One area in poor shape therefore pulls the headline down sharply and cannot be averaged away by stronger domains, although the weakest domain does not set the headline on its own.
boilerplate.exec_indicative: The grade is an early read of where OT security stands and where to look first. It does not verify controls in technical depth; the detailed assessments it points to do that.
boilerplate.not_determination: This is not a conformance assessment against ISA/IEC 62443 or any other standard, and it is not a regulatory determination. It is a structured interview carried out at a point in time, and the grade should be confirmed by the more detailed assessments it points to.

gov.purpose: Whether OT security is owned, understood as a risk, and supported by policy and management attention.
gov.why_it_matters: Without clear ownership and an accurate picture of the risk, OT security tends to be no one's job and gets attention only after an incident. Governance turns scattered good intentions into sustained effort and funding.

assets.purpose: Whether the organisation knows what it has in its OT environment and what is connected to it.
assets.why_it_matters: You cannot protect or monitor what you do not know is there. Incomplete asset and connectivity knowledge is one of the most common and most limiting gaps in OT, because every other control depends on it.

arch.purpose: How the OT environment is separated from other networks and divided internally, and how access and data crossing those boundaries are controlled.
arch.why_it_matters: Segmentation is the control that most limits how far a compromise can spread and keeps critical systems away from the routes attackers use. The architecture decisions made here shape how contained or how exposed an incident will be.

access.purpose: How identities and privileges are managed for the people and vendors who can reach OT systems.
access.why_it_matters: Shared logins, default passwords and standing broad access are common in OT, and they are what allows a minor foothold to become control of a process. Disciplined access control limits both accidents and attackers.

protect.purpose: The practical protective controls on OT systems: patching, malware protection, removable media, hardening and backups.
protect.why_it_matters: These are the day-to-day defences, and in OT they have to be applied with care for availability and for legacy systems that cannot always be patched. How they are actually applied on the systems counts for more than what the policy says.

monitor.purpose: Whether the organisation can see what is happening in its OT environment and would notice a problem.
monitor.why_it_matters: Many OT incidents run undetected because no one is watching the right signals. Without visibility a compromise persists and grows, and any later investigation becomes guesswork.

respond.purpose: Whether the organisation can respond to and recover from an incident affecting OT.
respond.why_it_matters: When prevention fails, the priority is to bring operations back quickly and safely. That depends on a response plan written for OT, engineering and security teams who already work together, and recovery that has been tested.

templates.low_confidence_flag: Overall coverage is below {coverageThresholdPct}. Treat this as a low-confidence initial read to be confirmed.
templates.domain_low_coverage: {domainName}: insufficient evidence to grade with confidence ({answered} of {scorable} answered). Indicative grade {domainGrade}, to be confirmed.
templates.all_top_band: Every question in this domain was answered at the top band; there are no lower-scoring points to note.

templates.headline_cap_note_unanimous: The top grade is awarded only where every domain reaches it, so the headline is held at {headlineGrade} even though the average is higher. The domains below the top grade are named in the results.
templates.headline_cap_note: The grade has been held down relative to the weakest domain, {weakestDomain} ({weakestGrade}), so a single weak area is not hidden by stronger ones.
templates.headline_cap_note_multi: The grade has been held down relative to the weakest domains ({weakestDomainsList}, all {weakestGrade}), so a cluster of weak areas is not hidden by stronger ones.
